content: 1. In lowand middle-income countries, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) are not recommended for diagnosing latent TB infection in children or for the diagnostic work-up of children suspected of TB disease, regardless of their HIV status. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 2. Commercial serodiagnostic tests should not be used in children suspected of having active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, irrespective of their HIV status. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence against the use of commercial serodiagnostics. 3. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients, including children, with presumptive or diagnosed TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 4. For the treatment of TB in children, the following daily dosages of anti-TB medications are recommended: Isoniazid (H): 10 mg/kg (range 7–15 mg/kg), maximum dose 300 mg/day. Rifampicin (R): 15 mg/kg (range 10–20 mg/kg), maximum dose 600 mg/day. Pyrazinamide (Z): 35 mg/kg (range 30–40 mg/kg). Ethambutol (E): 20 mg/kg (range 15–25 mg/kg). This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 5. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculosis peripheral lymphadenitis living in settings with low HIV prevalence and/or low isoniazid resistance, and who are HIV-negative, can be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for 2 months followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 4 months. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 6. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculosis peripheral lymphadenitis, or those with extensive pulmonary disease, living in settings with high HIV prevalence and/or high isoniazid resistance, should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for 2 months followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 4 months. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 7. Infants aged 0–3 months with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculosis peripheral lymphadenitis should be promptly treated with the standard treatment regimens described in recommendations 9 or 10. Dose adjustments may be required to account for age and potential toxicity. Decisions on dose adjustments should be made by clinicians experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 8. During the continuation phase of treatment, thrice-weekly regimens may be considered for children who are not HIV-infected and are living in settings with well-established directly observed therapy (DOT). This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence for intermittent treatment in children in specific settings. 9. Streptomycin should not be used as part of first-line treatment regimens for children with pulmonary TB or tuberculosis peripheral lymphadenitis. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 10. Children with suspected or confirmed tuberculosis meningitis or osteoarticular TB should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for 2 months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 10 months, for a total treatment duration of 12 months. The doses recommended for tuberculosis meningitis are the same as those for pulmonary TB. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 11. In settings where TB is highly endemic or where there is a high risk of exposure to TB, a single dose of the BCG vaccine should be given to all infants. The recommendation strength and evidence quality have not been graded. 12. In children known to be HIV-infected, the BCG vaccine should not be given. The recommendation strength and evidence quality have not been graded. 13. In infants whose HIV status is unknown, who are born to HIV-positive mothers, and who lack symptoms suggestive of HIV, the BCG vaccine should be given after considering local factors. The recommendation strength and evidence quality have not been graded. 14. Clinical evaluation of household and close contacts for active TB should be prioritized based on their risk of having or developing active TB or the potential consequences of the disease if it develops. Priority should be given to: Children with symptoms suggestive of TB. Children under 5 years of age. Children with known or suspected immunocompromising conditions, especially those living with HIV. Child contacts of index cases with multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant TB (proven or suspected). This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 15. Contact investigation should be conducted for household and close contacts when the index case has any of the following characteristics: Sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB. Multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant TB (proven or suspected). Is a person living with HIV. Is a child under 5 years of age. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 16. Contact investigation may be conducted for household and close contacts of all other index cases with pulmonary TB, in addition to the index cases covered in recommendation 19. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 17. Children under 5 years of age who are household or close contacts of people with TB and who, after appropriate clinical evaluation, are found not to have active TB should be given 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at 10 mg/kg per day (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day). This is a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence. 18. In settings of high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of people with TB should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 19. In settings of low HIV prevalence, all household members and close contacts of people with TB who have symptoms compatible with TB disease may be offered counseling and testing for HIV as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 20. All household contacts of an index case who is a person living with HIV should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 21. Children living with HIV who are more than 12 months of age, unlikely to have TB disease based on symptom-based screening, and have no contact with a TB case should: Be offered 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg per day, range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day) as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services if living in settings with high TB prevalence. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Might be offered 6 months of IPT as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services if living in settings with medium or low TB prevalence. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 22. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculosis peripheral lymphadenitis living in settings with high HIV prevalence (or with confirmed HIV infection) should not be treated with intermittent regimens (e.g., twice-weekly or thrice-weekly doses). This is a strong recommendation based on low to moderate-quality evidence against the use of intermittent treatment in children. 23. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculosis meningitis caused by multidrug-resistant bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone in the context of a well-functioning MDR-TB control program and within an appropriate MDR-TB regimen. The decision to treat should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 24. All children treated for TB should be recorded and reported by the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) in one of two age bands (0–4 years and 5–14 years). This recommendation is not graded and is based on good clinical practice.
